about: Advanced Sensor Systems (ASENS), FH Technikum Wien master's programme, 1st semester, after the slides of Kubinger (2020), ASENS_WS2020_Folien_v1_2Seiten.pdf, the multiple-choice control questions MC1.pdf and MC2.pdf (Fernlehre Kontrollfragen Teil 2 and Teil 1, WS2018), and the Intel RealSense D400 datasheet (Intel 2018) handed out as the lab manual (Manual.pdf). Pages are PDF pages of each file, read in their text layer on 2 Nov 2026; the slides hold two slides to a page, and the slide number is given beside the page. The past exams (WS2016, WS2017) ask only for explanations and sketches, and the MC sheets' ticks are not in their text layer, so no printed answer was taken from them; numbers printed in the slides are used where they exist, the rest were worked by hand from the slides' equations and say so. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes every answer with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.title: 3D sensors: time of flight and stereo

labs.title: Ranging by echo: ultrasound, RADAR, LIDAR
labs.idea: Send a pulse, wait for its echo, halve the path: the same rule ranges by sound and by light, and only the speed of the wave sets whether the wait is milliseconds or nanoseconds.

equations.note: Distance from the echo time t: out and back, so half the path. The slides state the halving for light in the ToF formula, d = c·φ/(4π·fmod) with φ/(2π·fmod) the round-trip time
Speed of sound in air; it depends on temperature, humidity and air pressure
Typical ultrasound frequencies, above human hearing

practice.question: A parking sensor hears its echo 5.8 ms after the burst. How far is the obstacle (sound at c0 = 331.6 m/s)?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 9 (c0) and p. 77 (the halving)

practice.question: The Velodyne HDL32 reaches about 120 m (slides p. 73). How long does the echo from 120 m take?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 73 (range 120 m) and p. 77 (the halving)
practice.solution: t = 2d/c = 240 m / 299 792 458 m/s = 0.80 µs: hence the very fast electronics a LIDAR needs (p. 70).

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 2: ultrasound pp. 8–10, RADAR pp. 13–15, LIDAR pp. 16–18; Modul 3: LIDAR pp. 69–76

labs.title: How much an image weighs: data and buses
labs.idea: Pixels times bytes per pixel is one image; times images per second, one camera's stream. A single colour camera already sends hundreds of megabits a second through the car.

equations.note: Bytes per image: width × height pixels × bytes per pixel (1 for 8-bit grey, 3 for 8-bit colour)
Bits per second for fimg images per second. The slides' example: 800 × 600 colour, ca. 1.5 MB per image, 25 per second, ca. 290 Mbit/s

practice.question: How much memory does one 1024 × 768 grey image (8 bit per pixel) need at least?
practice.source: MC2.pdf (MC Teil 1), Frage 2; 768 kBytes is among the printed options, the tick of the filled sheet is not in its text layer; worked by hand
practice.solution: 1024 × 768 × 1 B = 786 432 B = 768 × 1024 B: the option '768 kBytes', counting a kilobyte as 1024 bytes.

practice.question: One colour camera, 800 × 600 pixels, 3 bytes per pixel, 25 images per second: what data rate?
practice.source: Kubinger (2020), slides p. 35 (slide 70), printed: ca. 290 MBit/Sekunde
practice.solution: 800 × 600 × 3 B = 1.44 MB (ca. 1.5 MB); × 25 /s × 8 bit = 288 Mbit/s, the slide's ca. 290 Mbit/s.

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 2: data and buses pp. 35–36; MC Teil 1 (MC2.pdf), Frage 1 and 2

labs.title: The pinhole camera and its intrinsics
labs.idea: Each scene point reaches the image along a straight ray through one point, the projection centre. The intrinsic parameters fx, fy, cx and cy turn that ray into pixels; the ray alone cannot say how far the point is.
labs.law: u = cx + fx·xc/zc,  v = cy + fy·yc/zc

equations.note: The pinhole by the intercept theorem, in the positive position (plane in front of the centre, no mirroring)

equations.eq: u = cx + fx·xc/zc, v = cy + fy·yc/zc
equations.note: Image coordinates in pixels from camera coordinates in metres; fx, fy the focal length in pixels (a rectangular pixel has two), cx, cy the principal point
The calibration matrix
Its inverse
In homogeneous coordinates; back with K⁻¹ only if zc is known, since all points of a ray through the centre give the same (u, v)

practice.question: A camera has fx = 800 px and cx = 512 px. Where in u does a point at xc = 0.5 m, zc = 2 m appear?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 43

practice.question: Same camera (fx = fy = 800 px, cx = 512 px, cy = 384 px). A pixel at u = 700 px is known to lie 4 m deep. What is its xc?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 44 (K⁻¹)
practice.solution: xc = (u − cx)·zc/fx = (700 − 512) × 4/800 = 0.94 m. Without zc the pixel gives only the ray.

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: camera model pp. 39–44; MC Teil 1 (MC2.pdf), Fragen 3, 5, 7–10

labs.title: Where the camera stands: R, t and P
labs.idea: The extrinsic parameters, a rotation R and a translation t, carry a point from the world into the camera. Joined with K they make the projection matrix P: one product from world metres to pixels.

equations.note: World to camera coordinates, with Rᵀ = R⁻¹
And back
The projection matrix in homogeneous coordinates; s a scale factor

practice.question: A camera with fx = 700 px, cx = 512 px is not turned (R = I) and t = (0.2, 0, 1) m. Where in u does the world point (0, 0, 3) m appear?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides pp. 43 and 45

practice.question: The same camera, t = 0, is panned: R turns the world 30° about y, R = [cos 30° 0 sin 30°; 0 1 0; −sin 30° 0 cos 30°]. Where in u does (0, 0, 4) m appear?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides pp. 43 and 45

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: extrinsic parameters and the projection matrix pp. 42–46, calibration pp. 51–53

labs.title: Lens distortion, radial and tangential
labs.idea: A real lens bends straight lines, most of all far from the image centre and with short focal lengths. Five coefficients, k1, k2, k3 radial and p1, p2 tangential, describe it, and calibration finds them.

equations.note: The image point projected onto the plane z = 1 of the camera

equations.eq: xd = (1 + k1r² + k2r⁴ + k3r⁶)·xn, r² = xn² + yn²
equations.tex: \begin{pmatrix}x_d\\y_d\end{pmatrix} = \left(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4 + k_3 r^6\right)\begin{pmatrix}x_n\\y_n\end{pmatrix},\quad r = \sqrt{x_n^2 + y_n^2}
equations.note: Radial distortion, coefficients k1, k2, k3

equations.eq: xd = xn + p1·2xnyn + p2(r² + 2xn²), yd = yn + p1(r² + 2yn²) + p2·2xnyn
equations.tex: \begin{pmatrix}x_d\\y_d\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}x_n\\y_n\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}2p_1 x_n y_n + p_2\left(r^2 + 2x_n^2\right)\\ p_1\left(r^2 + 2y_n^2\right) + 2p_2 x_n y_n\end{pmatrix}
equations.note: Tangential distortion, coefficients p1, p2; usually negligibly small. The slides combine both models; the lab adds the tangential shift to the radially scaled point

practice.question: A point at xn = 0.4, yn = 0.3 through a lens with k1 = −0.2 (k2 = k3 = 0, no tangential part): what is xd?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 49
practice.solution: r² = 0.16 + 0.09 = 0.25; 1 + k1·r² = 1 − 0.05 = 0.95; xd = 0.95 × 0.4 = 0.38. Pulled inwards: barrel distortion.

practice.question: The same point with only tangential distortion, p1 = 0.01, p2 = 0: what is yd?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 49

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: lens distortion pp. 46–51; MC Teil 1 (MC2.pdf), Frage 6

labs.title: Colour models: RGB, HSI, HSV and grey
labs.idea: A colour camera gives R, G and B; models such as HSI and HSV split that into a pure colour (hue, saturation) and a brightness, so colour can be judged apart from light and shadow. Grey drops the colour, with green weighted most.

equations.note: HSI hue as a fraction of a turn; undefined when S = 0 or undefined
HSI intensity and saturation; S undefined when I = 0

equations.eq: V = max, Δ = V − min, S = Δ/V
equations.note: HSV value and saturation

equations.tex: H = \begin{cases}\frac{1}{6}\frac{G-B}{\Delta} & R = V\\ \frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{B-R}{\Delta}+2\right) & G = V\\ \frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{R-G}{\Delta}+4\right) & B = V\end{cases}
equations.note: HSV hue, by which channel is largest; 1 added when negative. Much faster than HSI
Grey with more weight on green; or I = (R+G+B)/3 with all alike

equations.tex: R = R_{u,v},\quad G = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(G_{u+1,v} + G_{u,v+1}\right),\quad B = B_{u+1,v+1}
equations.note: The primary Bayer pattern turned into colour, one 2 × 2 cell

equations.eq: R = YE − ½(G+G), G = ½(G+G), B = CY − ½(G+G)
equations.tex: R = YE - \tfrac{1}{2}(G + G'),\quad G = \tfrac{1}{2}(G + G'),\quad B = CY - \tfrac{1}{2}(G + G')
equations.note: The complementary pattern, with CY = G + B and YE = R + G

practice.question: What is the HSV hue of (R, G, B) = (1, 0.5, 0), in degrees?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 64

practice.question: What is the HSI saturation of (R, G, B) = (0.6, 0.3, 0.3)?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 63

practice.question: What grey value Y (green weighted) does (R, G, B) = (0.2, 0.6, 0.4) give?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 65

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: colour cameras pp. 54–65; exams WS2016 GrA and WS2017 GrB, Frage 1 (colour space models)

labs.title: The time-of-flight camera
labs.idea: A ToF camera lights the scene with modulated near-infrared light and every pixel measures the phase of what comes back. The phase gives the distance, but only up to half the modulation wavelength: beyond it the reading wraps round.

equations.note: Phase from four samples of the returned light; the lab takes the signs of both differences into account, so φ covers a full turn
Distance from the phase
The unambiguous range. The slide's example, λmod = 15 m at fmod = 20 kHz, holds for 20 MHz; λmod = c/fmod is worked here from that pair

practice.question: A ToF camera modulates at 20 MHz. What is its unambiguous range dmax?
practice.source: Kubinger (2020), slides p. 78 (slide 156), printed: λmod = 15 m (for '20 kHz', a slip for 20 MHz); dmax = λmod/2
practice.solution: λmod = c/fmod = 3·10⁸ m/s / 20·10⁶ Hz = 15 m; dmax = λmod/2 = 7.5 m. At 20 kHz λmod would be 15 km.

practice.question: At fmod = 20 MHz a pixel reads A1 = 1.5, A2 = 1.0, A3 = 0.5, A4 = 1.0. How far is the object?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 77

practice.question: The same camera looks at a wall 10 m away. What distance does it report?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides pp. 77–78
practice.solution: The phase wraps every dmax = 7.495 m, so 10 m reads as 10 − 7.495 = 2.51 m: a far wall seen as near.

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: time-of-flight cameras pp. 76–82; WH-Klausur WS2017 GrA, Frage 1; MC Teil 2 (MC1.pdf), Fragen 11–12

labs.title: Stereo: depth from disparity
labs.idea: Two calibrated cameras a baseline apart see a point at slightly different columns; that disparity gives the depth by triangulation. Depth falls as one over the disparity, so the farther the point, the coarser each pixel's step.

equations.note: Depth from the baseline b, focal length f and disparity d (f and d in the same unit, e.g. pixels)
So the depth resolution worsens with distance
The other two coordinates once zc is known
The depth one pixel of disparity spans, worked from zc = b·f/d
Field of view across n pixels of pitch p, worked from the pinhole; it reproduces the table's FOVh and FOVv
The invalid depth band at the left edge of a stereo module, seen by the left camera only

practice.question: The table of p. 87: f = 12 mm, b = 0.1 m, smallest disparity 2 px. Taking a pixel pitch of 7.68 µm (what the table's numbers imply), how far is zmax?
practice.source: Kubinger (2020), slides p. 87 (slide 173), printed: zmax = 78.13 m
practice.solution: f = 12 mm/7.68 µm = 1562.5 px; z = b·f/d = 0.1 × 1562.5/2 = 78.13 m. With the stated 6 µm it would be 100 m.

practice.question: Same table, f = 4 mm and b = 0.45 m, largest disparity 200 px, now with the stated 6 µm pixel. What is zmin?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides pp. 86–87; the slide prints 1.17 m, which needs 7.68 µm

practice.question: What horizontal field of view do 1024 pixels of 6 µm give behind a 4 mm lens?
practice.source: Kubinger (2020), slides p. 87 (slide 173), printed: FOVh = 75.0°

practice.question: A stereo head with b = 0.12 m, f = 4 mm and 3 µm pixels looks at a point 10 m away. How much depth does one pixel of disparity span there?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 86

practice.question: A D415-type module (baseline 55 mm, Manual p. 32) streams 1280 pixels across with a horizontal depth field of view of 65°. How many pixels at the left edge have no depth for a wall 1 m away?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Intel (2018), Manual.pdf p. 57; the 65° is this question's own value

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: stereo cameras pp. 82–97; exams WS2016 GrA and WS2017 GrB, stereo vision; MC Teil 2 (MC1.pdf), Fragen 13–16; Intel (2018), sections 2.3 and 4.7

labs.title: Finding the match: SAD and SSD
labs.idea: Stereo depth needs, for each point of the left image, its partner in the right one. A small window is compared at every shift along the row; the smallest sum of differences wins, unless the surface has no texture to compare.

equations.note: Sum of squared differences; the smaller, the better the match
Sum of absolute differences; the smaller, the better

equations.eq: d* = argmin over d of c(L(x), R(x − d))
equations.note: The disparity chosen, searched along one row because rectified images put corresponding points on the same row

practice.question: Two windows read (10, 20, 30) and (12, 18, 35). What is their SAD?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 87

practice.question: And their SSD?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 87
practice.solution: 4 + 4 + 25 = 33: SSD punishes the one large difference more.

practice.question: Left row 10 10 12 40 90 60 20 15 15 30 70 30 10 10 10 10; the right row is the same moved 3 places left. Searching d = 0 … 5 with a window of 5 around column 8 (counting from 0), which disparity wins by SAD?
practice.source: Worked by hand from slides p. 87
practice.solution: At d = 3 the right window equals the left one exactly, so its SAD is 0 and no other shift is as small.

labs.lecture: Kubinger (2020), Modul 3: correspondence, epipolar geometry and rectification pp. 87–91; MC Teil 2 (MC1.pdf), Fragen 17–20
